content: For individuals diagnosed with type 2 diabetes who are either overweight or obese, it is strongly recommended to achieve and maintain a weight loss of at least 5% of their total body weight. This level of weight reduction can be accomplished through a structured program that integrates nutritional guidance, increased physical activity, and behavioral therapy. Such an approach has been demonstrated to improve blood sugar control and cardiovascular health, reduce the risk of diabetes-related complications, and, in some cases, lead to remission of diabetes. High-frequency behavioral interventions are particularly recommended, with a minimum of 16 counseling sessions over a six-month period. These sessions should focus on critical components such as dietary modifications, increased physical activity, and behavioral changes. The goal is to facilitate sustainable lifestyle adjustments. Evidence supports that these intensive interventions are highly effective in promoting weight loss and fostering long-term healthy habits. To enhance accessibility and overcome barriers to participation, it is advised that these structured behavioral programs be offered in both in-person and remote formats. Dietary plans should be tailored to the individual, taking into account their unique needs, preferences, medical history, energy requirements, and specific weight loss objectives. Personalizing dietary recommendations in this way enhances adherence to the plan and motivates patients to achieve their weight-related goals. When developing a care plan, healthcare providers must also consider systemic and structural factors that may influence a patient’s ability to adhere to a weight loss regimen. These factors include food insecurity, cultural norms, and broader social determinants of health. Addressing these barriers is essential to creating an inclusive and supportive environment that facilitates successful weight management.
